records.title: Show HN: Stoke Money – Personal finance app built around a cash flow forecast
records.author: _wesley
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I've been through many finance tracking apps, starting with Personal Capital, then Monarch, and most recently Copilot. None of them have worked perfectly for my needs.

All of these apps tend to model “cash flow” as the net sum of your transactions during a month, yet while credit card charges are reported immediately, they are typically deducted from checking (cash) accounts the following month when the bill is due. As a result, I've always had to maintain a separate spreadsheet to track my actual cash flow.

These apps also have a huge focus on managing budgets, which has never been for me. My spending is rarely consistent month-to-month, so every month I'm comparing my fully justified spending against my budget, and tweaking my budget until I “pass”.

So I built yet another finance tracking app. It has the usual components - accounts, transactions, categories - but the core is a cash flow projection engine, and everything else is built around it.

Budgets are gone. Instead, each income/spending category is projected forward from your historical activity, but not as a flat monthly number. They land in whatever account you historically use (e.g. checking account for paychecks/rent/bills, credit/debit cards for daily spending). Credit card payments are modeled automatically based on your projected credit card balance. You can set up your own recurring transfers between accounts as well, to model savings, for example.

The end result is that the app can forecast how your cash moves, and you can see in advance when any account might run low. If all of your accounts look good for the next 12 months, maybe you don't have a budgeting problem.

What’s made the biggest difference for me has been the MCP integration, which I have connected to Claude (but can be connected to any AI agent of your choice). I have asked it to import historical transactions by uploading PDF account statements, categorize/tag all transactions that took place while I was on vacation, and plan transfers across my accounts to cover expected payments.

I hope some people that share my frustrations will find this app useful.

records.title: Show HN: I got tired of btop not seeing my Mac's chip, so I built siltop
records.author: cloaky233
records.storyText:
btop is beautiful. But on my M-series Mac it can't tell me the one thing I actually want to know: what is the chip doing? No watts, no GPU, no per-core clocks.

So I built siltop: btop's calm, with eyes on the silicon. Real power, clocks and temps straight from the SMC and IOReport, no sudo, about 1.3% of one core (btop is ~2.5% on the same machine).

It also tells you what's wrong in plain words ("Busy: rustc using 9.1 cores", "Hot: fans at 80%") before you read a single graph.

10-second try, no load needed:

  brew install cloaky233/tap/siltop && siltop --demo
Rust, MIT/Apache, no telemetry, no network unless you turn on update checks.

Curious what your Mac shows. M1/M2 Ultra and M5 Max owners especially, I haven't seen yours yet.

records.title: Show HN: Donut Browser, the most private anti-detect browser
records.author: andrewzeno
records.storyText:
Hi everyone!

About 2 years ago, I began to work on Donut Browser as a tool to manage browser profiles, which over time has evolved into a proper anti-detect browser.

Anti-detect browsers let you create browser profiles that look like as if you have a completely different computer. I believe Donut is the most private anti-detect browser because: - It has no telemetry and doesn't track your browsing activity - It spoofs your browser identity in a way that looks like a real device for every profile - It notifies you when a website takes a snapshot of your browser identity - It is built on top of Chromium and lets you block ads and trackers at the DNS level without relying on Manifest V2 - It lets you create unlimited profiles (the first anti-detect browser to do that) - It supports Linux, which not all anti-detect browsers do!

I use Donut as my main browser and the only other browser I have installed is Tor. If you are into privacy, it offers a lot better experience than Firefox containers or writing your own scripts to manage profiles!

If anyone is going to try it, would love to hear any feedback!

records.title: Show HN: Gondwana, a code-first C#/.NET game engine with WebGL
records.author: isthimius
records.storyText:
Gondwana is a 2D/2.5D game engine for C#/.NET 8 that I’ve been building over the past 16 months, using SkiaSharp for rendering. I've spent my career creating web and distributed apps and that has influenced the engine's development, so it will feel very familiar to anyone with a similar background. The engine is deliberately code-first in its implementation but still includes visual authoring tools and a custom CLI.

I started creating Gondwana to host my own RTS and SNES-style games, to offload the game ideas percolating in my brain. I wanted to focus more on creating gameplay systems and was less concerned with 3D graphics. The predictability and transparency of the old Win32/GDI era were the ideal for what I was shooting for, but I also wanted something faster and more portable than GDI32. To that end, I am not trying to emulate the bigger engines.

Spot! became my primary dogfooding project that I’ve since pushed up to itch.io. Getting a game to that point really helped burn away the cruft that accumulates from trying to create something like this. I was able to get Spot! to render at a consistent 120 fps on my dev machine. I experienced the absolute ecstasy of getting WebGL to cooperate with the engine cycle. And I discovered that even if Gondwana is code-first, you don’t want to hand-code platformer levels, so I added Gondwana Studio to the repository. Studio uses the same file formats that are understood by the core engine. Asset handling was beefed up, UI widgets were added for things like game HUD elements and engine diagnostics, and I fleshed out the CI/release pipeline to keep it organized.

As it stands currently, Gondwana supports GPU-backed OpenGL rendering with WinForms and Avalonia hosts, and a dedicated WebGL path with Blazor. Recently a good bit of effort has been put into optimizing the rendering hot-path, reducing contention between simulation and presentation, and into making the visual tooling easy to use by people other than just me. I even was able to get itch.io deployment down to a single command in the custom CLI.

The engine is still actively evolving feature-wise, but the core rendering is pretty solid right now. I expect Gondwana will remain 2D/2.5D with parallax support, so I am not trying to supplant Unity, Godot, et al. Also worth noting, Gondwana intentionally does not have an explicit ECS framework built in, although one could absolutely work well with the engine if desired.

The project is MIT licensed, the source is hosted on GitHub, the packages are on NuGet, and Spot! is playable in the browser at itch.io. I will include several links in the first comment under this. I’d love to see what other hobbyists or indie game devs think of the project. Feedback on usability, as well as praise and/or criticism of the architecture would be awesome.

records.title: Show HN: Sill for Android – control your Mac's windows from an Android phone
records.author: rahimnathwani
records.storyText:
Sill (discussed here: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50112739) streams one Mac window, or the whole Desktop, to an iPhone or iPad and lets you control it by touch. It's open source, so I made an Android client for it. It's unofficial and not affiliated with Sill's author: it speaks Sill's existing protocol, so the Mac side is the stock Sill app, unchanged.

Install Sill on the Mac, sideload the APK from Releases onto an Android 11+ phone on the same Wi-Fi, tap your Mac in the list that shows on your phone, then look for the 12-digit code in Sill on your Mac, and type it into the Android app.

Then: tap to click, drag to scroll, hold-and-drag to select text or move windows, pinch to zoom the picture on the phone, a Draw toggle for whiteboard apps like tldraw, and a key row with Esc, Tab, Cmd/Ctrl/Option/Shift and arrows. It also works over Tailscale with Sill's Remote Access.

All of the code was written by Claude Code, working from Sill's Swift source and its Python test client; I tested it on a Pixel 9 Pro XL.

Not done yet: drawing the Mac's pointer, a trackpad mode, clipboard sync, and a Play Store listing (I don't have Play developer account, and new individual Play developer accounts can't publish their first app until they've tested an app with a closed test with 12 testers.)

(There's also a separate Android client in draft PR #89 on Sill's repo. This one is a standalone app with an installable APK. I should have checked the issues/PRs before I asked Claude to build this...)

records.title: Show HN: CoastMath: (Open Source) Personal Finance and Retirement Planner
records.author: jfrbfbreudh
records.storyText:
Self-hosting instructions in the README.

Hosted version: https://coastmath.com/

iOS app: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6809539979

This post is partially inspired by this thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50048344

``` > Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt.

>> No, they can't, at least not any semblance of quality. The cases we're seeing where this does kinda work is in ports and translation where all the rules are already documented in the best specification language possible with a way for the LLM to verify itself: code. We saw this close to a year ago now with Cloudflare and NextJS ```

This post mostly outlines how I am personally building with agents, as I am almost entirely hands-off.

Desired feature-set determined by having agents research existing products and feedback / feature requests on FIRE subreddits.

Features built using Opus 5.5 (xhigh) / Fable 5.1 (med/high) as orchestrator and Opus-5-5 low/medium as worker subagents.

Quality is attempted by running Opus-5-5 agents in a perpetual audit + fixer loop on the calculation / compliance engine until no medium+ severity can be found. The origin of each rule / logic must be backed up and documented in the codebase with a source.

Sonnet subagents run UX / QA audit on iOS simulators within the Claude Code desktop app, and Opus agents resolve all medium+ sev issues; also run on a perpetual loop.

I have not manually tested or used the app(s) for more than 30 minutes. For UX quality, agents' screenshots + associated context are fed to a combination of GPT / Gemini / Claude agents until consensus is achieved on quality (7/10+).

Early feedback from beta testers report extremely close results to Boldin / Projection Lab. There is also a feature to import your data from Boldin and Projection Lab into CoastMath if you wish to compare the results yourself.

There is also a SimpleFIN integration, if you wish to pull in your own transaction data and see how your financial future changes based on your monthly spending habits (e.g. when I will get to retire if I spend like I did in June vs. July?).

I'm sure there are other features I don't yet know about. Again, I've barely used the app.

Anyway, feel free to use / roast / steal. I don't think that any moat can exist in this class of products in the future (where the rules are laws that are visible to everyone) and I don't expect to turn a profit.

Estimated cost: maybe $2000 if done over the API? I did most of this using the $200 Max subscription.

records.title: Show HN: Putaway – sorts your Mac's Downloads into the folders you have
records.author: yashrajpandey
records.storyText:
My Downloads folder is full of files like download (3).pdf, IMG_4821.jpg, and Untitled.docx. I already have folders for them in Documents. I never move them because I have to open each file to know what it is. Putaway does that part.

It reads the start of each file on your Mac: PDF text, OCR for scans and photos, Word, Excel, CSV, and HTML. Then it picks one of the folders you already have. It never makes new folders. It shows you the plan first. Nothing moves until you click Move, and Undo puts everything back.

Demo (this run uses a SubQ key, so some files are ready to move): https://github.com/devYRPauli/putaway/blob/main/docs/demo.gi...

You choose the model. The default is Apple Intelligence on your Mac. It is free, and nothing leaves your Mac. You can also use your own model through any OpenAI-compatible server, such as Ollama or LM Studio. Or you can add your own SubQ or Jev API key. Those two give a probability for each folder, so Putaway moves the files they are sure about. With Apple or your own model, you confirm each file.

I tested the released build on 107 files with messy names: public IRS forms, papers, receipts, photos, and spreadsheets, plus fake secret files and a partial download. There were 19 target folders, including decoy folders that apps make, such as Zoom and Adobe. Files in an acceptable folder: SubQ 88%, Jev 85%, qwen2.5 7B in Ollama 82%, Apple's on-device model 67% (of the 99 files it agreed to read). When SubQ or Jev moved a file on its own, it was right 132 of 136 times.

One surprise: Apple's on-device model refused to read three blank government forms, including the IRS 1040, as unsafe content. Putaway leaves those files in place and tells you why.

It never reads files with names like .env, id_rsa, or recovery-codes.txt. If a file's text looks like a private key or a token, it does not send it. It never overwrites a file, and it skips downloads that are not complete.

Install (Apple Silicon, macOS 26). The install script is 33 lines, so you can read it first:

  curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/devYRPauli/putaway/main/install.sh | bash

  brew install devyrpauli/tap/putaway
It is a Swift menu bar app and a CLI, MIT-licensed, with no dependencies. I do not pay for an Apple developer account, so the app is not notarized. The curl and brew installs do not show the Gatekeeper prompt.

I want to know which files it puts in the wrong folder, and which file types it misses. Keynote, Pages, and pptx files are filed by name only for now.

records.author: rochansinha
records.storyText:
Pomoflow is (yet another) Pomodoro app in a 1-bit style inspired by the early Macintosh GUI. It also has a todo list you can sync between your devices without having to login to an account. A jukebox loads and plays your favourite YouTube playlists. And there are bonus weekly focus stats for the numberphiles among us.

I built this because I wanted three things in one place: a pomodoro timer that looks good, a task list that syncs across my devices without an account (the apps I tried kept putting sync behind a login or a paywall), and my YT playlists I could play without having to leave the tab.

A little more detail on the no-account task list syncing- To sync tasks you generate a random 128-bit key and paste the key or scan a QR code on the other device. The pairing link carries the key in the URL fragment, so the browser never sends it to the server, and the server stores only a SHA-256 hash of it. Anyone with the key can read and edit the list. Without a key, tasks stay in the browser.

I prompted Claude to build a simulation using three.js, then added the relay visualization & then the ladder logic. Finally, I asked Claude to refactor the code & add descriptive documentation for readability.

records.title: Show HN: Animated step-by-step hints for any cryptic crossword clue
records.author: hiroprotag
records.storyText:
Cryptic crosswords are fun AND hard, and I've recently been introducing easier ones to my 11y/o daughter. It made me realise that when you're stuck, all you can do is hope you somehow come up with the way to crack it, or look at the answer and have all the satisfaction of figuring it out yourself removed!

I also realised that when I was explaining to her how clues worked, I would scribble all manner of letters, arrows doodles to make sense of how the words of the clue could be mangled and eventually produce the answer.

So I made a thing that would replicate the pencil and paper solving process, and create stepped visual animations that would enable you to get just enough info to make solving it within your reach, so you could feel like you did enough of the working out to get that "Aha!" feeling, without just getting straight to the answer.

You can paste in any cryptic clue with its length, e.g. "Around Los Angeles, coatless dudes make AI model, say (6)", and the animation shows you how to solve it, one step at a time. It's split into 3 or 4 sections, which most cryptic clues fit into:

1. Which end of the clue is the definition 2. What type of clue is it (there are several conventions in the cryptic world, a clue can be 1 of these, or a combination of several) 3. What are the pieces used to build the answer 4. How do the pieces fit together to create the answer

You can stop as soon as you have enough info to get you back to solving it yourself.

It was easy to get a smart AI to solve the clue - but it was trickier to get it to be reliable and correct. LLMs can be very good at writing a confident, plausible breakdown for a completely wrong answer! So I needed to use a multi-pass approach:

1. A small, fast model checks that the input looks like a cryptic clue. 2. A more capable model solves it and writes a step-by-step breakdown. 3. Another independent model solves it "blind", without seeing the first attempt or its answer. 4. A "judge" then checks that the two solvers agree on the answer and method, and that the letters in the breakdown actually add up to the answer.

If that fails, it tells you it’s unsure instead of bluffing, and if it’s only fairly sure that the answer and "how to" is the correct one, it says so.

The breakdown of how the clue is solved is then drawn as an animation, step by step, with letters and meanings scribbled and manipulated the way you'd do if you solving it yourself on paper.

Depending on the complexity, a clue usually takes between about 10 to 30 seconds to be solved. There's a cache, so clues that have already been solved once can be returned without going through the AI process again. It can still get things wrong, especially on loose clues or ones with some flexibility in how they can be interpreted, but generally it performs pretty well.

Your first clue solve is free, and an account gets you two more. There are paid plans to cover the AI costs involved for multiple solves as there is a cost to it.

There's also some good resources for learning cryptic crosswords basics - and a library of clues with hints to practice with. You can also write and share your own cryptic clues - along with the hint animation generated for them https://crypticinkling.co.uk/create

I’d love feedback from any cryptic crossword ninjas or beginners alike.

PS here's the breakdown for the clue at the top of this post: "Around Los Angeles, coatless dudes make AI model, say (6)" - how many hints do you need to crack it? https://crypticinkling.co.uk/clues/1hi0s2x

records.title: Show HN: I turned my kids' old Yoto Player into an Audiobookshelf player
records.author: beret4breakfast
records.storyText:
My kids love their Yotos and I love Audiobookshelf. I wanted something in between that works as they get older and more control. I had two old Gen 2 players lying around that Yoto no longer supports.

It turns the player into an Audiobookshelf client. You browse your library with the two knobs, the 16x16 screen shows tiny cover art, and favourites and downloads sync back to the server. Its still keeps the NFC card concept, but they're optional: you can link books/favourites to any NFC card. It all runs locally, with no Yoto account or cloud.

It does require opening the player and soldering some wires to flash the initial firmware, but then its OTA after that.

Disclaimer: Its all Claude Code, Its an idea I've been slowly tinkering around in my spare time and never got very far so. I threw Claude Code at it and I was amazed at how well it did. Flashing, reading logs and fixing things - leaving me to just perform physical button presses and checks.

records.title: Show HN: Pogi – AWS, Google Cloud and Azure on your machine, in one binary
records.author: narendev
records.storyText:
I built pogi to test cloud code locally without an emulator per service or a test account. It's one Go binary that serves 181 services across AWS, Google Cloud and Azure on one port.

The official SDKs, CLIs, Terraform and the CDK work unchanged, and there's a web console, IAM checks, chaos rules, snapshots built in and much more...

Some services are deep, others cover the common calls; the coverage page is honest about which. MIT licensed, no account. It's v0.1.0, so I'd love to hear what breaks.
